claims.text: Adding 1–3 at.% yttrium to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding 1–3 at.% yttrium will enhance the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
Conventionally processed phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys tend to crystallize during cooling.
Conventionally processed phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys exhibit a narrow supercooled-liquid region.
Yttrium has a large atomic-size mismatch relative to the other constituent atoms in the proposed alloys.
The yttrium addition will increase chemical and topological disorder and promote atomic-packing frustration.
Increased chemical and topological disorder and packing frustration will increase the nucleation barrier for crystallization.
Size-mismatched yttrium atoms will induce local structural distortions.
The yttrium-induced distortions will inhibit crystalline-phase nucleation and growth during cooling.
Yttrium will stabilize the amorphous structure by retarding atomic mobility.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the yttrium-modified alloy will have a wider supercooled-liquid region.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the yttrium-modified alloy will have a higher glass-transition temperature.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the yttrium-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature.
Relative to the undoped baseline, the yttrium-modified alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation.
Exceeding the optimal rare-earth concentration may diminish the benefit by causing secondary-phase formation.
The intervention may fail when the base composition is outside a regime in which atomic-size mismatch can inhibit crystallization effectively.
Very rapid or very slow cooling may diminish or override the proposed nucleation-inhibition effect.
Controlled melt-spinning of otherwise comparable undoped and 1–3 at.% yttrium-doped samples can test the proposed effect using DSC, XRD, TEM, and critical-cooling-rate measurements.
